title: EA-CORPORA-40 — The Fortieth Seating: Philology Constituted — Classical Philology 1906–1922 Whole, the Discipline Defined from Wolf to Usener, the Method from Lachmann to Housman, the Quarrel over the Geburt der Tragödie, the Standing Question from Valla to Bentley, Diels, Sandys, and the Census of Classical Philology
creator: Cranes, Rebekah
description: The fortieth seating of the originals shelf, sixteen seats, gathered for the census of the philology journals, which began with Classical Philology, and seated before it. Classical Philology I–XVII (1906–1922) whole, as JSTOR's Early Journal Content; the discipline defined: Wolf's Prolegomena ad Homerum (1795) and Darstellung der Alterthums-Wissenschaft (1807), Boeckh's Encyklopädie (1877), Usener (1882); the method: Lachmann's Lucretius (1850), Madvig's Adversaria critica (1871–1873), Housman's Manilius II (1912); the boundary drawn: Nietzsche's philological writings and Rohde's Afterphilologie (1872); the standing question: Valla, Casaubon (1614), Bentley (1699); Diels's Doxographi Graeci (1879); Sandys's History of Classical Scholarship (1903–1908); and the census of Classical Philology, without abstracts. Pointers to what is not seated, Wilamowitz's Zukunftsphilologie! first.

wiki_article: EA-CORPORA-40 is the fortieth seating of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's originals shelf, deposited under Rebekah Cranes, the standing authority on the EA-CORPORA deposits, on 16 November 2026. Titled Philology Constituted, it gathers sixteen seats for the census of the classical philology journals, which began with Classical Philology after that journal declined ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ, and it is seated before the census it serves. Classical Philology's first seventeen volumes (1906–1922) are seated whole, item by item, from JSTOR's Early Journal Content at the Internet Archive, so that a census that Crossref allows only from titles can read the text on the page. The discipline's constitution follows: F. A. Wolf's Prolegomena ad Homerum (1795), which made one name into many, and his Darstellung der Alterthums-Wissenschaft (1807), which bounded the object to Greece and Rome and set the Egyptians, Hebrews and Persians apart; Boeckh's definition of philology as the knowledge of what has been known (1877); and Usener (1882). The method is held in Lachmann's Lucretius (1850), Madvig's Adversaria critica (1871–1873) and Housman's Manilius II (1912). The boundary the field drew is held in Nietzsche's philological writings and Rohde's Afterphilologie (1872), the quarrel over the Birth of Tragedy; the canon of the standing question in Valla on the Donation of Constantine, Casaubon on the Hermetica (1614) and Bentley on Phalaris (1699); and the field's history of itself in Diels's Doxographi Graeci (1879) and Sandys's History of Classical Scholarship (1903–1908), where Wolf's matriculation as Studiosus Philologiae in 1777 is told as an epoch. The census of Classical Philology, without abstracts, is the sixteenth seat. Wilamowitz's Zukunftsphilologie! and the works not yet located are pointed to.
